The predictive comparison does not discriminate between models that imply different shares. The most useful next step is real-time scoring on data vintages, which would also give an evaluation that does not reuse the window.

12 Production-model history and switch rules

The production model was m9 (structural correlation and measurement SV) until 17 October 2026. It became m12 (adding AR(1) errors) and then, a day later, m13 (adding latent SV). Each switch rule was written down before the candidate’s comparison results were known, and every model-switch condition in Table 17 was met. The m12 → m13 rule added a fifth condition because m13 was a post-hoc candidate. The condition requires the z ≥ 2 margin to hold when every LFO refit uses its first sampling attempt, so that no retry with a new seed can create the margin. m13 needed no retry, so the condition changed nothing. The comparison author recommended treating m13 as a leading candidate rather than switching automatically, given the thin margin; the pre-set rule decided.

The move of the production sample to 1980 Q1 was not governed by a rule. The author of the comparison recommended keeping the full sample; the move was the project owner’s decision, taken on RDP 2014-12’s rationale. The prediction evidence was below the bar used for model switches, and the latent path barely moved. The decision rests on RDP 2014-12’s argument that early measurement errors are unrepresentative, and on the evidence in Section 8.1 that pre-1980 data inflate the constant-variance models’ error variances.

13 Diagnostics

All stored LFO fits meet the refit rule (Table 20). On the full sample the weakest-mixing fits are those trained on data ending just after COVID, where the constant-latent-variance models’ latent standard deviation mixes slowly. Weak mixing is not confined to those models: m13 has 2 weak-mixing fits on the full sample and 1 on the 1980 sample, all trained on data ending before 2020. On the 1980 sample the first attempt of m4’s refit to 2016 Q2 failed badly (E-BFMI 0.011, R-hat 1.28); its second attempt passed. The diagnostics table records each fit’s lowest bulk ESS but not the variable that has it.

14 Filter tests

Every filter used in estimation or evaluation is tested against a dense multivariate-normal computation (Table 21; 306 expectations in all, none failed). For m13 the tests check:

  • the Stan Kalman filter’s total and per-period log-likelihood against the dense multivariate-normal density of \(y\) (to \(10^{-9}\)), for five settings of \(\psi\) including \(\psi = 0\), equal \(\psi_E = \psi_I\) and \(|\psi|\) up to 0.95, with non-constant \(g\) and \(h\), a jump of +5 in \(g\), very small variances and extreme \(z_{EI}\);
  • bit-identity with m12’s filter when \(\tau_t\) is constant;
  • FFBS draws against the dense smoother (20,000 draws; worst mean error about two Monte Carlo standard errors);
  • the C++ filter used for LFO against the Stan filter (to \(10^{-11}\)) and against the fit’s stored predictive log-likelihood on posterior draws;
  • the particle filter against the exact Kalman filter as the volatilities of volatility go to zero, against m12’s particle filter at \(\omega_g = 0\), and against brute-force Monte Carlo over 200,000 simulated \((g, h)\) paths with a latent-volatility jump. The bootstrap and adapted proposals gave -37.488 and -37.497 against a brute-force value of -37.496 (standard error 0.005).

Equivalent tests exist for m12, m3 and m10 and for the Kalman filters of the linear-Gaussian models. For the tighter-prior variant, tests/test_m13_tight.R checks that its filter code is byte-identical to m13’s and returns identical output, and that at the same point (mapped between the two parameterisations) its log density differs from m13’s only by the difference of the priors, on the 1980-sample data.

15 Withdrawn results

The project’s record keeps superseded claims next to their corrections. The following were withdrawn and play no part in this paper.

  • PSIS-LOO rankings. “m9 is best by LOO, 6.3 nats ahead of m4”; “SV gains about 240 nats”; an hours-model gain over m8 by LOO. These were invalid for the reasons in Section 6.
  • “Latent growth is 30–35% less variable than headline.” This was the variance of the posterior-mean path. The per-draw measure is in Section 7.5.
  • The old m10’s scores and variance ratio. These came from a fit in mode A (Section 4.3); its particle-filter estimate for that mode did not converge in the particle count.
  • “m9 fixes m4’s bimodal persistence.” The bimodality was a sampler artefact.
  • “The measurement-SV gain largely disappears from 1980.” This rested on two non-nested comparisons, m9 − m5 (+16.7, z 1.13) and m4 − m1 (+28.2, z 1.46). m9 drops the serial correlation that m5 has, and m4 adds a latent AR(1). The nested comparisons give the “roughly halves” result in Section 7.7.
  • “m13 is the only three-measure model that keeps COVID in latent growth on both samples.” The constant-variance models also keep most of it there (Figure 6).

16 Reproduction

Every number in this paper is computed when the document is rendered, from four sources: paper/data/*.csv, output/tables/*.csv, output/sample_1980/tables/*.csv and docs/*.json|csv. The CSVs in paper/data/ are extracted from the local fit objects by paper/build_inputs.R; no model is fitted there. Three of them are transcriptions rather than extractions, and say so: rdp2014_reported.csv (values published in RDP 2014-12), record_facts.csv (facts recorded only in the project’s research log or Stan file headers, each with its source) and test_counts.csv (parsed from the test logs).

To rebuild from scratch:

  1. Rscript R/01_fetch_data.R and Rscript R/01b_fetch_research_data.R (data; the ABS may have released a newer vintage).
  2. The research suite on the full sample: Rscript R/02_fit_models.R, Rscript R/fit_m11.R, Rscript R/fit_m12.R, Rscript R/fit_m13.R (seeds 1 and 2, and --omega_g_sd=1), then Rscript R/03_compare.R (several hours).
  3. The same on the 1980 sample, with LATENTGDP_START=1980-03-01 LATENTGDP_OUT=output/sample_1980 (drivers in output/sample_1980/).
  4. Rscript R/fit_production.R (the production fit).
  5. The analyses added for this paper: Rscript paper/fit_rdp_sample.R (RDP-sample fits, output in output/sample_rdp/), Rscript paper/fit_rdp_sample.R --end=2019-12-01 --out=output/sample_rdp/end2019 m2 m13 (fits ending in 2019 Q4), LATENTGDP_START=1980-03-01 LATENTGDP_OUT=output/sample_1980 Rscript R/fit_m13.R --omega_g_sd=1 --out=output/sample_1980/fit_m13_omegag1.rds (prior sensitivity on the production sample) and Rscript paper/ppc_m13.R (predictive checks). The driver output/sample_rdp/run_new_analyses.sh runs the fits in order. The tighter-prior variant: Rscript paper/prior_candidates.R (prior predictive choice), bash output/sample_1980/run_tight.sh (its fits on seeds 1 and 2 and on the RDP sample, through R/fit_m13.R --variant=tight and paper/fit_rdp_sample.R m13_tight), Rscript tests/test_m13_tight.R and Rscript paper/ppc_m13.R --variant=tight.
  6. Rscript paper/build_inputs.R (about a minute), then quarto render paper/latentgdp_wp.qmd.

Steps 1–4 are documented in the repository’s README. The fits are large (about 0.1–0.3 GB each) and are not committed; the tables and the CSVs in paper/data/ are small and can be.
